knowledge_base_edges.mechanism: Jet fuel / ATF is refined from crude, so its price tracks crude plus a refining crack spread.
India imports most of the crude it consumes, so a higher price raises the import bill for given volumes.
Fuel and transport costs feed into consumer prices directly and via second-round effects.
Gasoline is a component of US CPI, so crude prices pass through to headline inflation.
Producers sell crude at prices linked to benchmarks, so realisations rise with the oil price.
When retail fuel prices are held steady, higher crude costs squeeze state-run OMC marketing margins.
Refining margins depend on the spread between product and crude prices, not the crude level itself.
Solvents, monomers and other crude derivatives are priced off crude.
Russia is a major crude exporter; higher prices raise export revenue for given volumes.
Front-month Brent futures price the international crude benchmark directly.
WTI futures track the US crude benchmark, which co-moves closely with Brent.
USD/INR is quoted as rupees per dollar, so a weaker rupee shows up as a higher USD/INR rate.
Fuel is typically one of the largest airline operating-cost items.
A larger oil import bill widens the trade deficit and hence the current account deficit.
Higher inflation reduces the RBI's room to cut and can raise expectations of tighter policy.
Higher inflation prints lead markets to price a tighter Fed path.
US energy-sector earnings rise with realised oil prices.

model_compatibility.reason: Its shock inputs describe the PAST 5 sessions. A slider describing a hypothetical future move cannot be fed into them without changing their meaning; on the 2023-2026 test it does not beat the zero or training-mean baselines.

Inputs are trailing 5-session moves; a hypothetical shock can only be read as 'the shock already happened last week', which excludes the immediate reaction. The model also shows no skill: its test MAE is not distinguishable from the zero-return baseline.
